turn_text: Well, thank you for having me to that. I really appreciate it.

There is so much going on now that has to do with appropriations, with agriculture, with a number of other areas. I know that you are going to chair the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Agriculture. And I just wonder if you'd give me an overview to begin with of how serious our issues are at this time of having an interim farm bill, not having budgets, and not having real assurance for people in agriculture of what is to come this year.

Yeah, I think they're very serious right now and I guess to step back and try to get a big picture view of this. I mean, the Congress has done a very poor job over the last few years of getting a budget. Everybody's talking about, you know, Obama hasn't had a budget in three years. Truth is there are two years in prison. Bush didn't have a budget either. And those are just kind of excuses. I mean, we all need to work better. Everybody's responsible for this. It starts at the White House, but really both houses and Democrats and Republicans are all responsible and we all share in the blame for this. And it's really too bad. And what you're seeing is kind of just that the grid lot is literally hurting America because you take how this will impact, let's just take one sector of agriculture, which is what your listeners are interested in. This is going to hurt American agriculture. We can talk about the sequestration if you want to in a minute. with just the lack of budget clarity, the lack of ability to plan and to know what's coming up for farmers and agribusants around the country. USDA can't make any long-term plans. It's just not a good circumstance, and it's not a good way to govern. So I'm very concerned about it, but at the same time, You know, hopefully this year is going to be better than the last couple of years. There's some very positive signs in the Senate about us working in a more bipartisan way. That's, you know, when I ran for the Senate back in 2002, that's what I talked about the whole time. I ran ads on it. I went all of a state talking about bipartisanship. I've tried very hard to be very bipartisan. And I'm hoping that the American people that had enough of this partisan gridlock is red versus blue. Excuse me, red versus blue game you get up in Washington and I'm hoping people are not going to tolerate it anymore and we'll basically send a very clear message to Washington that we want y'all to get along. We want you to work together and we want to find solutions like with agriculture. We had a farm bill last year in the Senate and we passed it big by parts of the vote. I actually go against it. I didn't support it but I was glad we did work on it and about parts of the way and it got passed went over to the house and it died on the vine over in the house. Yeah, hopefully this year will be better. It's really, from my standpoint, it's just really a matter of political will. If we have the will to do it, we can do all this stuff. It's hard politically, but it's not hard, you know, mathematically. You know what you have to do, and you know the process, and we know that we should be doing better.
Senator, saying all of this, do you think sequestration will kick in in March?

I've been, I've tried to be the eternal optimist on sequestration and say that it would not kick in, but I'm going to tell you, this last week in Washington was pretty gloomy because it looks like between the House and Senate and, you know, again, you know that there's going to be a problem because the blame game started full speed ahead this week with, you know, House and Senate Republicans blaming Obama and then Democrats blaming the Republicans You know, that's a total road to nowhere. But when you hear that kind of stuff come out of Washington, you know that people are just positioning to try to, you know, get a political advantage over this. But the bottom line is that sequestration will come into effect unless we act. And we don't have long to act. We just have a couple of weeks to act on this. So we had a hearing yesterday in the Senate Appropriations Committee. And we had three cabinet level secretaries, and then we had someone from the Department of Defense and someone from OMB, the Office of Management and Budget. And that's the executive branch's version of the CBO. But nonetheless, that we sat there and pummeled down with questions for two, two and a half hours. And I'm going to tell you, sequestration is bad. It's going to be bad for US economy. It creates a lot of hardships. And with all due respect to the national news media, the way they sort of a position that are phrased, that are framed it up nationally, is they said, well, it's going to be X amount of federal spending cuts. And that's true on its face, but you need to look at a context and what happens out there in the US economy. So one example that we talked about quite a bit in my office is the meat inspectors. Now, we take these people for granted. These are federal government employees. We take them for granted. We have the safest and best who's fly in the world. And we just kind of take it for granted, everything works like it should, but those meat processing plants cannot function unless they have a meat inspector there on the premises. So now if you're going to have to start furloughing meat inspectors, what does that mean to the toxins of the world and the pilgrims of the world and all that? They're not going to be able to run their plants, but they don't have a meat inspector in the plant. Certainly you're talking about a chain reaction of layoffs, a disruption to the food supply, and the ripple effects just go on and on. So this is much broader than several billion dollars in the federal government. This is really going to be an economy-wide problem for the U.S.
